--- format: clean-revealjs: css: misc/slides.css smaller: true execute: echo: true eval: false cache: true --- ::: {.cell} ::: # Supervised Classification
in Remote Sensing {.r-fit-text .titlepage} ## Learning Objectives {.smaller} By the end of this lesson you will be able to: - Describe the **supervised classification pipeline**: from labelled ground truth polygons to a full raster map - Explain the **polygon-to-point sampling step**: why it is needed in this workflow and what it implies for class balance and spatial autocorrelation - Explain the **spatial autocorrelation problem** and why it makes standard accuracy estimates misleading - Explain the role of **feature extraction** as the bridge between raster data and any ML algorithm - Explain why **pixel brightness alone** often fails, and how **spatial texture** addresses this limitation - Distinguish **overall accuracy, producer's accuracy, and user's accuracy** — and what each tells a map-maker # Introduction {.subtitle} ## What makes RS classification different? - **Spatial structure**: pixels are not independent — spatial autocorrelation matters - **Scale of prediction**: we predict on entire rasters (millions of pixels), not just point datasets - **Spatial sampling**: ground truth comes from polygons, requiring careful sampling strategies - **Feature engineering**: spatial context (focal operations) is critical, not just pixel values :::{.notes} These differences are why we can't just apply generic ML tutorials to RS data! The spatial workflow (`terra`/`sf` packages) and understanding spatial autocorrelation are essential skills, regardless of whether you use classical ML or deep learning. ::: --- ### Data - Historic aerial imagery from 1961 ([swisstopo](https://map.geo.admin.ch/#/map?lang=de¢er=2706292.97,1144053.16&z=9.82&bgLayer=ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe&topic=ech&layers=ch.swisstopo.swissimage-product_1946,f;ch.swisstopo.swissimage-product@year=1961)) - Single band (grayscale), 0.5 m/pixel resolution - Images available for: 1961, 1971, 1977, 1983, 1989, 1995 - Ground truth forest polygons (hand-digitized) ## {background-iframe="https://map.geo.admin.ch/#/map?lang=de¢er=2706292.97,1144053.16&z=9.82&topic=ech&layers=ch.swisstopo.swissimage-product_1946,f;ch.swisstopo.swissimage-product@year=1961&bgLayer=ch.swisstopo.pixelkarte-farbe" background-interactive=true} --- ![](img/ces-grey.png) ## Workflow Overview 1. Load ground truth polygons and generate point samples 2. Spatial train/test split (⚠ autocorrelation) 3. Extract raster features using `extract()` 4. Train classifier (CART for interpretability) 5. **Predict on entire raster** 6. Evaluate and compare approaches # Ground Truth & Spatial Sampling {.subtitle} ## From polygons to points {#sec-spatial-sampling} Unlike standard ML datasets, our ground truth comes as **spatial polygons**. :::{layout-ncol=2} ![](img/ces-grey.png) ![](img/ces-poly.png) ::: --- We need point samples for training: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load polygons library(sf) ces_polygons <- read_sf("data/ces_polygons.gpkg", "ces_polygons") study_area <- read_sf("data/ces_polygons.gpkg", "study_area") ``` ::: []{} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Generate spatially distributed samples sample_points <- st_sample(ces_polygons, 1000) |> st_sf() ``` ::: []{} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Attach class label to each point labelled_data <- st_join(sample_points, ces_polygons) |> select(-jahr) labelled_data$class <- factor(labelled_data$class) ``` ::: --- ![Sample points from forest (green) and non-forest (orange) polygons](img/ces-samples.png) --- **`st_sample()`** draws random points *within* each polygon geometry. **`st_join()`** does a spatial left join — for each point it finds the polygon that contains it and copies over the attributes (`class`, etc.). Result: an `sf` data frame where every row is a labelled point with known coordinates. :::{.notes} `st_join()` is a spatial equivalent of `dplyr::left_join()`. Instead of matching on a key column it matches on spatial containment/intersection. The `-jahr` drop is just to keep the data frame clean — `jahr` is the digitizing year, not useful as a feature. ::: --- ## Train/test split: The spatial autocorrelation problem :::{.callout-important} **Spatial autocorrelation issue**: Random splits violate independence assumptions because nearby pixels are correlated. Proper approaches use spatial cross-validation [@brenning2023; @schratz2021]. We use random splits here for simplicity, but be aware this may overestimate performance. ::: :::{.notes} **Pedagogical simplification**: Random train/test split **Production approach**: - Spatial k-fold cross-validation with geographic blocking - Ensures training and test data are spatially separated - Packages: `sperrorest`, `mlr3spatiotempcv`, `CAST` - More realistic performance estimates ::: --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(42) idx <- sample(nrow(labelled_data), floor(0.7 * nrow(labelled_data))) data_train <- labelled_data[ idx, ] data_test <- labelled_data[-idx, ] ``` ::: - 70 / 30 split is a common heuristic - `set.seed()` makes the result reproducible - Both sets **retain their geometries** — we still know where each point is on the map # Approach 1: Single-Band Classifier {.subtitle} ## Feature extraction {#sec-feature-extraction1} `terra::extract()` samples raster values at each point location: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_features <- terra::extract(ces1961, data_train, ID = FALSE) data_train2 <- cbind(data_train[,"class"], train_features) |> st_drop_geometry() ``` ::: :::{.notes} `ID = FALSE` drops the row index column that terra adds by default. `st_drop_geometry()` removes the spatial geometry — the ML model doesn't need coordinates, only the feature values. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 2 class luminosity 1 Non-forest 0.635 2 Forest 0.208 3 Forest 0.396 4 Forest 0.298 5 Forest 0.129 6 Non-forest 0.698 7 Forest 0.0863 8 Non-forest 0.741 9 Forest 0.325 10 Forest 0.275 ``` ::: ::: --- ## From spatial to tabular After feature extraction, the spatial complexity is gone — we have a plain data frame: | class | luminosity | |---|---| | Forest | 0.38 | | Non-forest | 0.74 | | Forest | 0.41 | | … | … | From here, **any standard ML algorithm applies**. The spatial awareness is only needed again at prediction time, when we apply the model back to the full raster. --- ## Training {#sec-training-model1} We use CART (decision trees) for interpretability. As experienced ML practitioners, feel free to substitute with Random Forest, XGBoost, etc. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(rpart) cart_model <- rpart(class ~ luminosity, data = data_train2) ``` ::: :::{.notes} **Pedagogical choice**: CART for transparency **Production alternatives**: - Random Forest / XGBoost: Better accuracy, handles non-linearity - Support Vector Machines: Good with limited training data - Neural Networks: Requires more data but state-of-the-art performance CART lets students see *exactly* what decision boundaries the model learned. ::: --- ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Decision tree for single-band classification](lesson4_files/figure-revealjs/fig-cart-basic-1.png){#fig-cart-basic width=960} ::: ::: --- ## Raster prediction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Predict probability per class for all pixels ces1961_predict <- predict(ces1961, cart_model, type = "prob") # Get highest probability class ces1961_predict2 <- which.max(ces1961_predict) ``` ::: --- ## How `terra::predict()` works Conceptually: iterate over every pixel, build a one-row data frame of its values, call `predict(model, newdata = ...)`, write the result back. ``` for each pixel (i, j): features <- extract value(s) at (i, j) probs <- predict(model, newdata = features, type = "prob") output[i, j] <- probs ``` - Output of `predict(raster, model, type = "prob")`: one **layer per class**, values = probabilities - `which.max()` returns an integer raster: which layer has the highest probability? --- ## Setting categorical levels `which.max()` returns **integers** (1, 2, …). To get meaningful labels: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} classes_df <- data.frame(id = 1:2, class = levels(data_train2$class)) levels(ces1961_predict2) <- classes_df ``` ::: - The layer order matches the **alphabetical order** of factor levels in the training data - Without this step the result raster only contains 1s and 2s --- ![Classification result — single band approach](img/ces-predict.png) --- ## Evaluation {#sec-model-evaluation-1} Before showing the numbers: **how to read a confusion matrix** | | Actual: Forest | Actual: Non-forest | |---|:---:|:---:| | **Predicted: Forest** | TP | FP | | **Predicted: Non-forest** | FN | TN | - **Overall accuracy** = (TP + TN) / total - **Producer's accuracy** (recall) = TP / (TP + FN) — "of actual forest, how much did we catch?" - **User's accuracy** (precision) = TP / (TP + FP) — "when we predict forest, how often is it right?" :::{.notes} Overall accuracy is misleading when classes are imbalanced (e.g. 90% non-forest): a model that always predicts non-forest gets 90% accuracy. Producer's accuracy matters for the map-maker ("is my map complete?"). User's accuracy matters for the map-user ("can I trust this label?"). ::: --- ::: {#tbl-confusion-matrix-basic .cell tbl-cap='Confusion matrix for single-band classification'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Actual
Forest Non-forest
Forest 137 22
Non-forest 55 87
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: **Overall accuracy**: 0.74 # The Spatial Context Problem {.subtitle} ## Why pixel-based classification struggles {#sec-spatial-context} - At pixel level, it is hard to distinguish forest from non-forest - Spatial context is essential: humans use texture, patterns, and neighborhoods to classify land cover ![](img/ces-crop.png){#fig-zoom-problem} :::{.notes} This is the **core limitation** of pixel-based classification. Modern deep learning (CNNs) solves this automatically by processing image patches, but we'll first show the manual approach to understand *why* spatial context matters. ::: # Approach 2: Adding Spatial Features {.subtitle} ## Focal operations as feature extractors {#sec-feature-engineering} **Focal operations** aggregate neighborhood values, providing spatial context: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} i <- 5 focal_window <- focalMat(ces1961, d = (i-1)/2 * res(ces1961)[1], type = "rectangle") # Standard deviation within each 5×5 neighborhood ces1961_focal_sd <- focal(ces1961, focal_window, fun = "sd") ``` ::: - **High SD** → heterogeneous neighborhood → likely a forest edge or textured canopy - **Low SD** → uniform neighborhood → likely open field or dense uniform forest :::{.notes} **Pedagogical approach**: Handcrafted focal features **Why we do this**: - Explicit, understandable feature engineering - Shows *what* spatial context means (texture/variation) - Works with classical ML algorithms **Production approach**: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) - CNNs learn optimal spatial filters automatically during training - First layer convolution weights = learned focal operations - Can learn multi-scale features (equivalent to multiple focal window sizes) - State-of-the-art: U-Net, DeepLabV3+, Vision Transformers ::: --- :::{#fig-zoom-comparison layout-ncol=2} ![Original raster](img/ces-crop.png) ![After focal SD filter — bright = high texture](img/ces-focal-crop.png) ::: --- ## Normalization for multi-feature learning When combining features with different scales, normalize to [0, 1] using min-max scaling: $$x' = \frac{x - \min(x)}{\max(x) - \min(x)}$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} minmax_normalization <- function(x){ minmax_vals <- minmax(x)[,1] (x - minmax_vals[1]) / (minmax_vals[2] - minmax_vals[1]) } ces1961_focal_sd <- minmax_normalization(ces1961_focal_sd) # Stack: now a 2-band raster ces_multi <- c(ces1961, ces1961_focal_sd) names(ces_multi) <- c("luminosity", "focal_sd") ``` ::: Why normalize? Decision trees are invariant to scale, but other algorithms (SVM, KNN, neural networks) are not. It's good practice regardless. --- ## Training with spatial features The call is identical — `rpart` just sees more columns now: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Same workflow, but data_train2_multi has two feature columns cart_model_multi <- rpart(class ~ ., data = data_train2_multi) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Decision tree now uses both luminosity and spatial texture](lesson4_files/figure-revealjs/fig-cart-multi-1.png){#fig-cart-multi width=960} ::: ::: --- ## Prediction and evaluation {#sec-model-evaluation-2} ::: {#tbl-confusion-matrix-multi .cell tbl-cap='Confusion matrix with spatial features'} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Actual
Forest Non-forest
Forest 175 37
Non-forest 17 72
````` ::: ::: **Overall accuracy**: 0.82 (vs. 0.74 without spatial features) --- ## What did we gain? | | Features | Overall accuracy | |---|---|:---:| | Approach 1 | luminosity | 0.74 | | Approach 2 | luminosity + focal SD | 0.82 | The texture feature captures **local variation** — forest canopy looks rougher at 0.5 m resolution than agricultural fields or roads. **One extra focal operation nearly free-rides on the existing workflow** — same model, same extraction, same prediction step. --- ## Further improvements For advanced applications, consider: - **More focal features**: mean, local range, edge-detection filters (Sobel, Laplacian) - **Multi-scale features**: focal operations at different window sizes (5×5, 15×15, 31×31) - **Deep learning**: CNNs learn optimal spatial filters automatically — no manual feature engineering - **Object-based classification**: segment the image first, then classify segments rather than pixels - **Proper spatial CV**: use spatial blocking for more realistic accuracy estimates :::{.notes} **Key message for students**: Our approach teaches the *concepts*: - Why spatial context matters - How to work with spatial data in R - The ML workflow for remote sensing In practice, you'd use deep learning frameworks (TensorFlow/PyTorch) with architectures designed for image segmentation. The concepts remain the same, but the implementation is more sophisticated. Good starting points: - `TorchGeo` (PyTorch for geospatial data) - `segmentation_models.pytorch` (pre-built architectures) - Papers: U-Net for RS, DeepLabV3+, attention mechanisms ::: ## References {#refs}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
